n: At dawn the full council met to make its decision official, then tied Jesus up and handed him over to Pilate. Under Roman rule, only the governor could carry out a death sentence.

f.g: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor (prefect) of Judea about AD 26-36.

n: Pilate asked, “Are you the King of the Jews?” — a political charge, since a rival king meant rebellion against Rome. Jesus answered, “You say so,” affirming it but not in Pilate’s sense.

f.g: A guarded yes — “those are your words.”

n: The chief priests piled on accusations, but Jesus said nothing.
Pilate pressed him: don’t you have any answer? Look how many charges they bring.
Jesus still said nothing, and Pilate was amazed. His silence fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy of the silent lamb.
It was customary at Passover for the governor to release one prisoner the people asked for.
A man named Barabbas was in prison with rebels who had committed murder during an uprising against Rome.

f.g: Aramaic “son of the father” — an irony, since Jesus is the true Son of the Father.
Rebellion, uprising.

n: The crowd began calling for Pilate to grant the usual Passover release.
Pilate offered to release “the King of the Jews.”
He realized the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of jealousy.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to demand Barabbas instead.

f.g: Stirred up, incited.

n: Pilate asked what they wanted done with the one they called King of the Jews.
They shouted, “Crucify him!”

f.g: Execute by nailing or tying to a cross — Rome’s most painful and shameful punishment, reserved for slaves and rebels.

n: Pilate asked what crime he had committed, but they only shouted louder, “Crucify him!” An innocent man was condemned by a mob.
Wanting to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas, had Jesus flogged, and handed him over to be crucified. The guilty went free while the innocent took his place — a picture of the Atonement.

f.g: Flogged with a whip of leather straps embedded with bone or metal — often brutal enough to kill.
Wanting to satisfy the crowd.

n: Soldiers took him into the governor’s headquarters and gathered the whole cohort.

f.g: The governor’s official residence in Jerusalem.
A cohort — a unit of up to 600 soldiers.

n: They dressed him in a purple robe — the color of royalty — and pressed a crown woven from thorns onto his head, mocking his kingship.

f.g: Woven, braided.

n: They saluted him mockingly: “Hail, King of the Jews!” — a parody of “Hail, Caesar!”
They beat him on the head with a reed (a mock scepter), spat on him, and knelt in fake homage. One day every knee will bow in true worship.
When they finished mocking him, they put his own clothes back on and led him out to be crucified.
Jesus was too weak from the scourging, so soldiers forced Simon of Cyrene, a passerby from North Africa, to carry the cross beam. Mark names his sons, likely known to Mark’s readers.

f.g: From Cyrene, a city in today’s Libya with a large Jewish community.

n: They brought him to Golgotha, meaning “Place of a Skull,” just outside the city walls.

f.g: Aramaic “skull”; Latin Calvaria gives us “Calvary.”

n: They offered him wine mixed with myrrh, a drink that dulled pain, but he refused it, choosing to face his suffering fully conscious.

f.g: A bitter aromatic resin used as a mild narcotic.

n: They crucified him and divided his clothing by casting lots, fulfilling a psalm of the suffering righteous one.
It was the third hour — about 9 a.m. — when they crucified him.

f.g: Hours were counted from about sunrise; the third hour was around 9 a.m.

n: The charge written above him read, “The King of the Jews.” Meant as mockery, it was the truth.

f.g: Inscription — a placard listing the crime.

n: Two rebels or robbers were crucified with him, one on each side — the places James and John had asked for in glory.

f.g: Bandits, possibly rebels like Barabbas.

f.w: one on his right hand, and the other on his left

n: This fulfilled Isaiah’s words that he would be counted among the wrongdoers. (Many manuscripts lack this verse, but the prophecy is quoted in Luke.)

f.w: he was numbered with the transgressors

n: Passersby hurled insults, shaking their heads in scorn, mocking his supposed claim to destroy and rebuild the temple.

f.g: Insulted, reviled.

n: “Save yourself — come down from the cross!” But by staying on the cross he would save others.
The chief priests and scribes mocked too: “He saved others; he can’t save himself.” Unknowingly, they spoke a deep truth.

f.g: Not that he couldn’t, but that he wouldn’t — saving us required him to stay.

n: “Let the Christ come down now so we can see and believe.” Even the men crucified beside him insulted him.

f.g: Insulted, abused verbally.

n: At the sixth hour (noon), darkness covered the land until the ninth hour (3 p.m.). Creation itself mourned.

At three o’clock Jesus cried out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Latter-day Saint leaders have taught that the Father withdrew his Spirit so the Son could finish the Atonement alone.

f.g: Aramaic: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

n: Some bystanders misheard “Eloi” as a call for Elijah, whom Jews expected to come in times of need.

f.g: Elijah.

n: Someone soaked a sponge in sour wine and lifted it to his mouth on a reed, saying, let’s see if Elijah comes to take him down.

f.g: Sour wine, the cheap drink of soldiers.

n: With a loud cry, Jesus breathed his last. He voluntarily gave up his life; no one took it from him.

f.g: Breathed out his spirit — died.

n: The temple veil — the heavy curtain closing off the Holy of Holies — was torn from top to bottom. God himself opened the way into his presence through Christ.
The Roman centurion standing in front of the cross saw how Jesus died and declared, “Truly this man was the Son of God.” A Gentile soldier makes the confession Mark’s Gospel has been building toward.

f.g: A Roman officer commanding about 80-100 soldiers.

f.w: Truly this man was the Son of God

n: Women watched from a distance, including Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses, and Salome.

f.g: Mary from Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, healed by Jesus.
Probably the mother of James and John.

n: These women had followed Jesus in Galilee and supported his ministry; many others had come up with him to Jerusalem. When the men fled, the women stayed.

f.g: Served and supported him, including with their means.

n: Evening was coming on the day of preparation — Friday, the day before the sabbath. Bodies had to be buried before sunset.

f.g: The day to prepare for the sabbath — Friday.

n: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who was waiting for God’s kingdom, courageously went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. It took real boldness to be associated with a crucified man.

f.g: A town in Judea, probably northwest of Jerusalem.
Member of the council (Sanhedrin).
Asked for, requested.

n: Pilate was surprised Jesus was already dead — crucifixion often took days — and asked the centurion to confirm it.
Once the centurion confirmed the death, Pilate released the body to Joseph. Jesus truly died; his resurrection was not a recovery.
Joseph bought linen, took the body down, wrapped it, and laid it in a tomb cut out of rock. He rolled a stone across the entrance.

f.g: Tomb.

n: Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses watched where he was laid. They would be witnesses to the empty tomb, knowing exactly where it was.
